Dublin Food Sharing Initiatives

Multimodal screening report based on 83 candidate URLs and their supplied approximate coordinates

36 retained · 47 discarded · screening completed 15 August 2026

Geographic Distribution

The screening retained 36 initiatives from 83 candidate URLs, and 35 of those retained records contain complete coordinate pairs in the supplied dataset. Community Roots is the only retained record without a latitude in the CSV; its page places the organisation at the Guinness Enterprise Centre on Taylor’s Lane in Dublin 8, so it is included in district analysis but not plotted as a coordinate point. Using page-stated addresses where available and the supplied coordinates otherwise, Dublin 8 forms the largest retained district group, with seven initiatives including Bridgefoot Street Community Garden, Donore Community Drug and Alcohol Team, Dublin Food Co-op, Little Flower Penny Dinners and Mendicity Institution Food Service. Dublin 7 follows with five retained initiatives around Bow Street, Infirmary Road, Grangegorman, Cabra West and Phibsborough, combining meal support with community growing and student food redistribution.

Northern clusters extend through Finglas, Ballymun, Coolock, Raheny and Clontarf, represented by Finglas Forest Garden, Muck and Magic Community Garden, Northside Partnership Community Food Hub, St Anne's City Farm and St Anthony's House. South and south-west Dublin contain a second broad band of activity, including Airfield Community Garden near Dundrum, Muslim Sisters of Éire in Dublin 14, Mother McAuley Centre and WALK Community Gardens in Dublin 12, Ballyfermot Family Resource Centre Meals on Wheels in Dublin 10, and FoodCloud and Trustus Senior Care Meals on Wheels in Dublin 24. The eastern side is represented by Donnybrook and Clontarf services and by St Anne's City Farm in Raheny, while central Dublin contains several street-homelessness meal services close to Dublin 1, Dublin 2 and Dublin 8. The map uses the candidate coordinates exactly as supplied rather than correcting them to page addresses, because the coordinates were provided as approximate locations and some do not coincide precisely with the address described on the source page. The district bar chart therefore uses page-stated postal districts when explicit, supplemented by neighbourhood and coordinate inference where the page does not publish a district, so its counts describe the screened sample rather than official administrative boundaries.

Types of Food Sharing Initiatives

The 36 retained initiatives fall into four analytical types: 16 community-growing or garden-sharing projects, 16 prepared-meal or meal-support services, three food-redistribution, pantry or hub initiatives, and one co-operative food retailer. The growing group ranges from educational and shared gardens such as Airfield Community Garden and Mud Island Community Garden to garden-share activity through Community Roots / Soil Mates and disability-inclusive growing through WALK Community Gardens. The prepared-meal group includes fixed-site meal centres such as Capuchin Day Centre and The Light House, soup-run or street-outreach provision such as Muslim Sisters of Éire and Mustard Seed Soup Run, and older-person services that provide lunch or Meals on Wheels through Mary Aikenhead Day Centre, Mother McAuley Centre, Sancta Maria Day Centre, St Anthony's House and Trustus Senior Care Meals on Wheels. Food sharing within the community-growing category is often embedded in collective cultivation rather than formal food-aid distribution: Mud Island Community Garden states that planning, sowing and harvesting are shared and that produce can be taken as needed, while Summer Row Community Garden describes harvested produce being shared each week.

Other garden pages emphasise food production and horticultural learning, including Bridgefoot Street Community Garden with local organic vegetable growing, Finglas Forest Garden with annual vegetable beds and orchard planting, and Muck and Magic Community Garden with vegetables, fruit, composting and a polytunnel. The redistribution category is represented by FoodCloud, which connects surplus food with charities, ReFridge TU Dublin, which redistributes surplus FoodCloud supplies to TU Dublin students, and Northside Partnership Community Food Hub, whose linked food-club service combines low-cost food access with surplus-food repurposing. Dublin Food Co-op is distinct from the aid and garden models because it operates as a member-owned, not-for-profit consumer co-operative selling affordable and sustainably sourced groceries. The donut chart therefore assigns 44.4% of the retained sample to community growing and garden sharing, 44.4% to prepared meals and meal support, 8.3% to redistribution, pantry and hub activity, and 2.8% to co-operative food retail. These percentages describe the screened URL sample only and should not be interpreted as estimates of the true city-wide prevalence of each FSI type.

Operational and Funding Models

Community-led operation is most visible among the growing projects: Blarney Park Community Garden describes residents and local people collectively gardening disused Dublin City Council land, Mud Island Community Garden organises a shared community garden, and St Anne's City Farm states that the city farm is run entirely by volunteers. Council support appears without replacing community control in several cases, including Muck and Magic Community Garden on Dublin City Council land, Infirmary Road Community Garden on a Council site, and Hardwicke Street Garden Club, which works with Dublin City Council and employment-support programmes. NGO and charitable models dominate direct food-aid and meal services, including Capuchin Day Centre, Little Flower Penny Dinners, Sancta Maria Day Centre, The Light House, Mendicity Institution Food Service and Crosscare Community Cafés and Food Support. Public or programme funding is explicit for some of those organisations: FoodCloud identifies support through the Community Services Programme, while Mendicity Institution Food Service and Crosscare Community Cafés and Food Support identify European Social Fund Plus food support administered through Irish government structures.

Faith-linked voluntary provision is also prominent, with Muslim Sisters of Éire operating as an independent voluntary organisation, Mustard Seed Soup Run running a soup service for people living on the streets, and The Light House operating through Dublin Christian Mission in partnership with TIGLIN. Dublin Food Co-op uses a different governance model because its page describes a not-for-profit social enterprise owned by its members, with members participating in the co-operative rather than receiving charity services. Community Roots / Soil Mates is likewise presented as a social enterprise and company limited by guarantee, using structured garden sharing to connect people who have garden space with people who want to grow food. Mother McAuley Centre illustrates a mixed model: the centre was established through religious and parish collaboration, works with volunteers, receives assistance from statutory services, raises funds, and hosts a local Meals on Wheels service. The operational categories are therefore not mutually exclusive in practice, because several initiatives combine community management, charitable status, council land, statutory cooperation, programme funding or social-enterprise structures.

Reach and Activity

Capuchin Day Centre publishes the clearest large-scale recent activity figures in the retained set, reporting 331,300 hot meals, 77,300 food parcels and 6,545 infant parcels in 2025, alongside support for 1,073 families including 1,854 children. Mendicity Institution Food Service reports more than 50,000 meals per year through a free food service that provides breakfast and dinner six days a week to people experiencing homelessness. Dublin Food Co-op reports a community of more than 2,500 members supported by 120 volunteers and 18 staff, providing a rare membership-based measure of participation rather than a meal count. FoodCloud documents substantial redistribution through its Dublin history, including a period in which the Dublin Hub redistributed 567 tonnes of food to 325 charities, while later network figures on the page cover wider Ireland and United Kingdom operations rather than Dublin alone.

Activity evidence for Bridgefoot Street Community Garden is older but specific: its page records that a score or more of community groups, businesses and services had used the garden and lists a 2018 schedule of Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday opening sessions. Mud Island Community Garden provides current operational evidence through Tuesday and Saturday public opening from 14:00 to 17:00 and website news posts dated 4 and 7 August 2026. ReFridge TU Dublin states that its Grangegorman food pantry operates every academic week on Wednesdays from 15:30 to 17:30, while Trustus Senior Care Meals on Wheels offers Meals on Wheels on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays from 11:30. Little Flower Penny Dinners provides warm meals on weekdays at noon and operates Meals on Wheels 365 days a year, while the linked Northside Partnership Community Food Club page describes a ten-week pilot in which participants pay five euros per week for up to twelve food items. Several garden pages publish no visitor totals, so their activity is reported here through stated opening sessions, recurring programmes, volunteer structures, harvest practices or dated site updates rather than through invented attendance estimates.

Digital Presence and Accessibility

The retained initiatives range from actively maintained service websites to older project pages that function mainly as historical documentation, creating substantial variation in how current activity can be verified online. Mud Island Community Garden shows particularly current digital evidence, with news posts dated 4 and 7 August 2026 alongside public opening hours, while Dublin Food Co-op carries current co-operative information and 2026 member-facing material. Capuchin Day Centre publishes a recent 2025 impact summary with service totals, and Little Flower Penny Dinners maintains practical information on meal provision, Meals on Wheels and its annual National Food Bank Day campaign. By contrast, Bridgefoot Street Community Garden relies heavily on material dated 2018, Serenity Community Garden has a page last updated in 2020, and Heritage Community Garden is documented through a 2014 article, so those pages support existence and past operation more strongly than current activity levels.

Thirty-three of the 47 discarded URLs were inaccessible during screening, including several Facebook and Instagram pages as well as websites returning errors, blocked responses or unavailable content. Eight additional pages were discarded because the visited page did not describe a food-sharing initiative, three were directories or policy pages rather than standalone initiatives, two described activity outside Dublin city, and one described a supper-club activity that had ended. Among accessible retained services, pages such as Ballyfermot Family Resource Centre Meals on Wheels, Sancta Maria Day Centre, The Light House, Mendicity Institution Food Service and Trustus Senior Care Meals on Wheels publish concrete participation information such as opening days, meal schedules, service areas or contact details, making access conditions relatively easy to establish. Some retained community-growing pages, including Braithwaite Community Garden and Infirmary Road Community Garden, provide much less operational detail, so the screening can establish their identity and location more confidently than their present scale or frequency. The digital evidence therefore supports strong claims where pages publish dated schedules or metrics, but it requires explicitly historical wording where the only accessible material is old and prevents any inference about activity for URLs that could not be read.

Notable Initiatives

Capuchin Day Centre is notable for the largest recent quantified service volume published by a retained Dublin page, with its 2025 totals covering hot meals, food parcels, infant parcels and families supported from its Bow Street base. Dublin Food Co-op stands out structurally because it combines food access with member ownership, reporting more than 2,500 members, 120 volunteers and 18 staff in a long-running not-for-profit consumer co-operative. FoodCloud is notable for scaling a Dublin-origin surplus-food model: its history begins with a 2012 donation of unsold market food to Don Bosco Teenage Care and develops into a technology-supported redistribution network. Mud Island Community Garden offers a clear community-sharing model in North Strand because members collectively plan, sow and harvest, produce is available to take as needed, and the garden publishes twice-weekly public opening hours.

Bridgefoot Street Community Garden provides a strong example of reuse of urban space in the Liberties, combining community access with horticultural training and local organic vegetable growing and documenting use by numerous community groups and services. Northside Partnership Community Food Club is distinctive for combining a low weekly contribution with a choice of up to twelve food items, surplus-food repurposing through FoodCloud and complementary food-related workshops during its ten-week pilot. ReFridge TU Dublin adapts surplus redistribution to a university setting by using TU Dublin student organisations and FoodCloud supplies to stock a recurring campus pantry in Grangegorman. Hardwicke Street Garden Club illustrates a locally embedded garden model in the city centre, created by residents in 2010, focused on healthy food production, and supported through relationships with Dublin City Council, Gateway or Tús and community funding schemes. Mendicity Institution Food Service and Crosscare Community Cafés and Food Support are notable for coupling food provision with wider support systems: Mendicity combines free meals and food parcels with homelessness services, while Crosscare links community cafés and emergency food support with casework in several Dublin locations.
